question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

TENACIOUS
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Persistent.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Tenacious (adjective) means holding firmly to something and refusing to give up; determined and persistent. (दृढ़, हठीला)
◦ Example: Her tenacious pursuit of the case forced the department to reopen it.

 

• Persistent carries the same sense — continuing firmly in a course of action in spite of difficulty or opposition. (लगातार बना रहने वाला)
◦ Example: Persistent enquiry finally produced the missing file.

 

• The word comes from Latin tenere (to hold) — the same root as tenant, tenure, retain and tenacity. Anything tenacious holds on.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Yielding (नम्र, हार मानने वाला): giving way readily to pressure — the opposite of tenacious.

 

• Option 2: Irresolute (अनिश्चयी): unable to decide or hold to a decision — also an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Wavering (डगमगाता): hesitating between choices — again an antonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Note the design: three antonyms and one synonym. Fix the meaning of the given word first, then discard every option that agrees with the majority sense.

 

• Other synonyms of tenacious: dogged, resolute, steadfast, unwavering, pertinacious.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

OSTENTATIOUS
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Unassuming.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ostentatious (adjective) means characterised by a vulgar display of wealth, learning or success, designed to impress others. (दिखावटी, आडंबरपूर्ण)
◦ Example: The ostentatious decoration of the hall drew more comment than the ceremony itself.

 

• Its true opposite is unassuming — modest and not seeking to draw attention to oneself. (विनम्र, सादा)
◦ Example: For all his achievements he remained an unassuming man.

 

• The word comes from Latin ostendere, "to show" — the same root as ostensible (apparent, put forward as a reason) and ostentation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Showy (भड़कीला): attracting attention by being bright or elaborate — a direct synonym.

 

• Option 3: Flamboyant (आडंबरपूर्ण): confidently and strikingly showy in manner or appearance — also a synonym.

 

• Option 4: Flashy (तड़क-भड़क वाला): ostentatiously attractive in a cheap way — again a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other antonyms of ostentatious: modest, restrained, understated, plain, unpretentious.

 

• In SSC antonym questions the setter usually supplies three synonyms and one antonym. Identify the odd option out and confirm it against the meaning of the given word.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

To sit on the fence
option_1: To avoid taking sides in a dispute
option_2: To guard one's own property jealously
option_3: To wait idly while others do the work
option_4: To criticise a matter from a safe distance
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To avoid taking sides in a dispute.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "To sit on the fence" means to remain neutral and refuse to commit to either side of an argument or contest. (तटस्थ रहना)
◦ Example: Two members voted against the resolution while the rest sat on the fence.

 

• The image is of a person perched on the boundary between two fields, having chosen neither. The idiom usually carries a note of mild disapproval, since the neutrality is seen as evasive rather than principled.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 takes the fence literally as a boundary being guarded.

 

• Option 3 describes idleness, for which the idiom would be "to twiddle one's thumbs" or "to rest on one's oars".

 

• Option 4 describes safe criticism, nearer to "to be an armchair critic" — the commonest trap in this question.

 

NOTE

 

• Related idioms of commitment and neutrality: "To nail one's colours to the mast" (to declare one's position openly), "To run with the hare and hunt with the hounds" (to support both sides at once) and "To take the middle path".

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

SPURIOUS
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Genuine.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Spurious (adjective) means not what it purports to be; false or fake. It is also used of reasoning that appears sound but is not — a spurious argument. (नकली, मिथ्या)
◦ Example: The certificate was found to be spurious and the appointment was cancelled.

 

• Its true opposite is genuine — authentic; actually what it is claimed to be. (असली, प्रामाणिक)
◦ Example: Only genuine spare parts carry the manufacturer's seal.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Bogus (फर्जी): not real, though pretending to be — a synonym.

 

• Option 2: Counterfeit (जाली): made in exact imitation of something valuable in order to deceive — also a synonym.

 

• Option 4: Fake (नकली): not genuine; imitation — again a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other antonyms of spurious: authentic, bona fide, legitimate, veritable, valid.

 

• Note a useful technical sense: a spurious correlation in statistics is one that appears real but arises from a hidden third factor — a term that has begun to appear in comprehension passages.

question: Spot the correct spelling of the technique used to record the electrical activity of the brain.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Electroencephalography.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Electroencephalography", abbreviated EEG, is the technique of recording the electrical activity of the brain through electrodes placed on the scalp. It is used chiefly in the diagnosis of epilepsy and sleep disorders. (मस्तिष्क विद्युत-आलेखन)
◦ Example: Electroencephalography confirmed the abnormal discharge in the left temporal lobe.

 

• Break the word into its Greek roots: ELECTRO (electricity) + ENCEPHALO (brain) + GRAPHY (recording, writing). Reading long medical terms root by root is the reliable method in such questions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "Electroencaphalography" — incorrect; the root is "encephalo", with an e after the second c.

 

• Option 3: "Electroencephelography" — incorrect; the syllable is "phalo", not "phelo".

 

• Option 4: "Electroenchephalography" — incorrect; an extra "h" has been inserted after the second c.

 

NOTE

 

• Related recording techniques worth remembering: electrocardiography (ECG) for the heart, electromyography (EMG) for muscle, and encephalitis — inflammation of the brain — which shares the same encephalo root.

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitute for the given expression.

 

'A short pithy saying that expresses a general truth'
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Aphorism.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• An aphorism is a brief, memorable statement of a general truth or principle — compressed wisdom in a single line. (सूक्ति)
◦ Example: "Brevity is the soul of wit" is among the best-known aphorisms in English.

 

• The word comes from Greek aphorismos, a definition or distinction. Its defining features are brevity and generality — it states not a fact about one case but a truth about many.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Anecdote (किस्सा): a short amusing or interesting story about a real incident or person.

 

• Option 3: Allegory (रूपक): a narrative in which characters and events stand for abstract qualities or ideas.

 

• Option 4: Anagram (वर्ण-विपर्यय): a word or phrase formed by rearranging the letters of another.

 

NOTE

 

• Related literary one-word substitutes: Maxim and Adage (a traditional saying), Proverb (a popular short saying with advice), Epigram (a witty, often paradoxical statement), Paradox (a self-contradictory statement that may be true) and Euphemism (a mild word used for a harsh one).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

___ of the two proposals was found acceptable by the board, and both were returned for revision.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Neither.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The rule turns on how many items are involved:

◦ "Neither" and "either" are used for exactly two.
◦ "None" and "any" are used for more than two.

 

• The sentence says "the two proposals", so only neither or either is possible. Since the second clause states that both were returned, a negative sense is required, which gives "Neither".

◦ Correct: Neither of the two proposals was found acceptable.
◦ Compare: None of the seven proposals was found acceptable.

 

• Note also that "neither of" takes a singular verb — was, as in the sentence.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: None — correct in sense but wrong in number; it is reserved for more than two.

 

• Option 2: Either — right for two, but affirmative, which contradicts the second clause.

 

• Option 3: Any — used for more than two, and normally in questions and negatives.

 

NOTE

 

• The same two-versus-many distinction governs several pairs: between (two) and among (more than two); either/neither (two) and any/none (more than two); the former/the latter (two) and the first/the last (more than two); better (of two) and best (of more than two).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

___ examining the samples, the inspector ordered the entire consignment to be withheld.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. On.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The structure "On + gerund" means immediately after doing something. It is a compact substitute for a clause beginning with as soon as or when.

◦ Correct: On examining the samples, the inspector ordered the consignment to be withheld.
◦ Equivalent: As soon as he examined the samples, the inspector ordered …
◦ Example: On reaching the office, she found the file already cleared.

 

• The subject of the gerund must be the same as the subject of the main clause — here the inspector both examines and orders — otherwise the participle dangles.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: At — used with a gerund only in fixed phrases such as good at swimming, not to mark a point in time.

 

• Option 3: With — would suggest accompaniment or instrument, which the sense does not require.

 

• Option 4: For — would express purpose or duration, again not the sense here.

 

NOTE

 

• Compare the two related structures: "On + gerund" means immediately after; "In + gerund" means while in the act of — In crossing the road, he dropped the file. SSC has set these two against each other more than once.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The ___ the deadline came, the more anxious the whole team became.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. nearer.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence uses the double comparative structure, in which two things increase or decrease together. Its fixed form is:

◦ The + comparative …, the + comparative …
◦ Example: The higher the fee, the fewer the applicants.

 

• The second half of the sentence already reads "the more anxious", a comparative. The first half must therefore also take a comparative, which is "nearer".

◦ Correct: The nearer the deadline came, the more anxious the team became.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: near — the positive degree, which cannot follow the in this structure.

 

• Option 2: nearly — an adverb meaning almost, unrelated to the sense required.

 

• Option 4: nearest — the superlative, which is used for the highest degree among three or more, not in a paired comparison.

 

NOTE

 

• Two well-known proverbs use this pattern: "The more, the merrier" and "The sooner, the better." Note also that the verb is often omitted in such short forms, but the two comparatives must always both be present.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The committee examined (1)/ the revised proposal (2)/ very careful before recommending it (3)/ to the general body. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (3).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The word in question modifies the verb "examined", telling us how the committee examined the proposal. A verb must be modified by an adverb, not by an adjective.

◦ Corrected sentence: The committee examined the revised proposal very carefully before recommending it to the general body.

 

• "Careful" is the adjective, used to describe a noun (a careful reader). "Carefully" is the adverb, used with a verb (read carefully).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct — the singular subject committee agrees with examined.

 

• Part (2) is correct — the revised proposal is a well-formed noun phrase.

 

• Part (4) is correct — to the general body uses the right preposition.

 

NOTE

 

• A few adverbs are worth watching, since the adjective and adverb differ in meaning:
◦ He worked hard (with effort) versus He hardly worked (scarcely at all).
◦ He arrived late (after time) versus He has not written lately (recently).
◦ After linking verbs — be, seem, appear, look, feel, taste, smell, sound — an adjective is correct: The soup tastes good, not well.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

He has been appointed (1)/ as an university lecturer (2)/ in the department of (3)/ modern Indian history. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The choice between "a" and "an" depends on the sound with which the following word begins, not on its spelling.

 

• "University" begins with the letter u but is pronounced "yoo-niversity" — that is, with the consonant sound /j/. It therefore takes "a", not an.

◦ Corrected sentence: He has been appointed as a university lecturer in the department of modern Indian history.
◦ Example: a European country, a one-rupee coin, a useful book, a unique opportunity.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct — the present perfect passive has been appointed is well formed.

 

• Part (3) is correct — in the department of uses the right prepositions.

 

• Part (4) is correct — no article is needed before an academic subject.

 

NOTE

 

• The rule works in the other direction too. Words beginning with a silent h start with a vowel sound and take "an": an hour, an honest man, an honour, an heir. Compare a hotel, a historic occasion, a horse, where the h is pronounced.

question:
Change the following sentence from active voice to passive voice.

 

The municipality collects the water tax every quarter.
option_1: The water tax was collected by the municipality every quarter.
option_2: The water tax has been collected by the municipality every quarter.
option_3: The water tax is being collected by the municipality every quarter.
option_4: The water tax is collected by the municipality every quarter.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The water tax is collected by the municipality every quarter.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is in the Simple Present Tense — structure: Subject + V1/V5 + object. The phrase every quarter marks it as a habitual action.

 

• The passive of the simple present is formed as: Object + is/am/are + V3 + by + Subject.

◦ Active: The municipality collects the water tax.
◦ Passive: The water tax is collected by the municipality.

 

• The auxiliary agrees with the new subject: the water tax is singular, so "is" is used, not are.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 uses "was collected", the passive of the simple past, which clashes with the habitual sense of every quarter.

 

• Option 2 uses "has been collected", the passive of the present perfect, presenting the action as completed.

 

• Option 3 uses "is being collected", the passive of the present continuous, which makes the action ongoing at this moment rather than habitual.

 

NOTE

 

• Time expressions are the quickest check on tense during voice conversion. Every day, usually, generally, often and as a rule point to the simple present; now, at present, at this moment to the present continuous; and already, just, yet, so far to the present perfect.

question:
Convert the sentence given below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure.

 

The tender had been cancelled by the department before the last date of submission.
option_1: The department had cancelled the tender before the last date of submission.
option_2: The department cancelled the tender before the last date of submission.
option_3: The department has cancelled the tender before the last date of submission.
option_4: The tender had cancelled the department before the last date of submission.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The department had cancelled the tender before the last date of submission.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is in the Past Perfect Passive — structure: had been + V3. Its active counterpart is the Past Perfect Active — had + V3.

◦ Passive: The tender had been cancelled by the department.
◦ Active: The department had cancelled the tender.

 

• In the conversion the agent after "by" becomes the subject, the original subject becomes the object, and the past perfect must be preserved, since it shows that the cancellation preceded the last date.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 uses the simple past, which loses the sequence of the two past events.

 

• Option 3 uses the present perfect, which cannot be combined with a completed past reference.

 

• Option 4 reverses the roles — the tender becomes the doer and the department the thing cancelled.

 

NOTE

 

• A useful check after every conversion: confirm that the doer of the action is still the doer. Option 4 illustrates the commonest slip, in which the two nouns are simply swapped without regard to sense.

question:
Select the sentence that contains the homophone of the highlighted word.

 

The syllabus for the refresher course was revised only last year.
option_1: The course was revised again in the following session.
option_2: She completed the course in June and joined the office.
option_3: The sand at that end of the riverbed is unusually coarse.
option_4: A refresher course for clerks begins next month.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The sand at that end of the riverbed is unusually coarse.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homophone is a word that sounds the same as another but is spelt differently and has a different meaning. (समोच्चारित किंतु भिन्न वर्तनी वाला शब्द)

 

• Course is a noun meaning a programme of study, a direction of movement, or a part of a meal.
• Coarse is an adjective meaning rough in texture, or crude and unrefined in manner. The two are pronounced alike, so "coarse" is the homophone required.

◦ Example: The rope was made of a coarse fibre that chafed the hands.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Options 1, 2 and 4 all reuse the same spelling "course" in the sense of a programme of study, so none of them supplies a homophone.

 

NOTE

 

• Memory aid: coarse describes something rough; a course is something you follow.

 

• Other adjective–noun homophone pairs asked in SSC: discreet/discrete, dessert/desert, sole/soul, medal/meddle, waist/waste and plain/plane.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

Music reaches its listeners today by two quite different routes, and each shapes what the music is allowed to be. A recording is made in fragments, assembled, corrected and then fixed. Its virtue is exactness: a wrong note can be removed, a tempo steadied, a balance adjusted until every instrument sits precisely where the producer intends. What the listener finally hears is a version that has never existed in a single unbroken moment, and one that will sound the same on every hearing for as long as the file survives.

 

A live performance offers the opposite bargain. Nothing can be corrected, and nothing will recur. The tempo shifts with the temper of the hall, a phrase is stretched because the audience has gone unusually quiet, and a small error passes unrepaired into the shape of the evening. Musicians describe the difference as that between a photograph and a conversation. The recording preserves; the concert responds.

 

Neither route is simply superior, though partisans of each speak as though it were. Defenders of recording point out that it democratised access: a listener in a small town can now hear performances once confined to a few metropolitan halls, and can hear them repeatedly, which is how most people actually come to know a piece. Defenders of live music reply that endless correction has bred a public intolerant of imperfection, and that a generation raised on flawless files now hears the small human unevenness of a concert as a fault rather than as the point.

 

The real question is not which format ought to survive. It is whether a culture that can afford both will go on valuing the one that cannot be edited. Access is easily measured and easily funded; the willingness to sit in a hall and accept whatever happens is neither, and it is the harder of the two to rebuild once it has been lost.

 

Which of the following best captures the essence of a recording, as described in the passage?
option_1: A live moment captured exactly as it happened
option_2: An exact, unchanging version assembled from separate fragments
option_3: A cheaper substitute meant for listeners who cannot attend concerts
option_4: A performance that varies slightly with every hearing
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. An exact, unchanging version assembled from separate fragments.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The first paragraph states that a recording is made in fragments, assembled, corrected and then fixed, and that its virtue is exactness.

 

• The author then draws out the consequence: what the listener hears is a version that has never existed in a single unbroken moment, and one that will sound the same on every hearing. Both halves of Option 2 come straight from these lines.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is the exact opposite of the passage's claim that no single unbroken moment is preserved.

 

• Option 3 introduces cost, which the passage never discusses.

 

• Option 4 describes the live performance, not the recording — the standard SSC trap of attaching the right description to the wrong item.

 

NOTE

 

• In a passage built on a two-way contrast, always check which of the two items an option is describing before checking whether it is true. Half the wrong options in such sets are accurate statements about the other item.

What criticism of recorded music is made by the defenders of live performance?
option_1: That it is too expensive for ordinary listeners
option_2: That it has reduced the earnings of working musicians
option_3: That it cannot reproduce sound with sufficient accuracy
option_4: That endless correction has bred a public intolerant of imperfection
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. That endless correction has bred a public intolerant of imperfection.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The third paragraph reports the reply of the defenders of live music: endless correction has bred a public intolerant of imperfection, so that a generation raised on flawless files hears the small human unevenness of a concert as a fault rather than as the point.

 

• The criticism is therefore about the listener, not about the technology. Recording is faulted for what it has done to expectations, not for any failure of sound quality.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Options 1 and 2 raise cost and musicians' earnings, neither of which appears in the passage.

 

• Option 3 reverses the argument entirely — the passage credits recording with exactness, and that very exactness is the ground of the complaint.

 

NOTE

 

• Where a passage sets out the case of two opposing camps, note who says what. Questions of this kind are answered from a single clause, and the phrase "Defenders of … reply that" marks exactly where to look.

According to the musicians quoted in the passage, the difference between the two formats is like the difference between
option_3: a letter and a telephone call
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. a photograph and a conversation.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The second paragraph states it directly: musicians describe the difference as that between a photograph and a conversation.

 

• The comparison is then compressed into four words that explain it: the recording preserves; the concert responds. A photograph fixes a moment permanently; a conversation adjusts itself to whoever is present.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Options 2, 3 and 4 are all plausible-sounding comparisons, but none of them appears anywhere in the passage.

 

• Option 3 in particular is a near miss — a letter and a telephone call would capture the same contrast between the fixed and the responsive, but the author did not use it.

 

NOTE

 

• Questions about a simile or metaphor are pure location questions: the image is a distinctive phrase sitting in the text. Do not judge which comparison is most apt — find the one the author actually used.

What is the author's attitude towards live performance?
option_2: Nostalgic to the point of rejecting recordings
option_4: Entirely neutral, with no view expressed
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Sympathetic but even-handed.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The author's sympathy is plain in the last paragraph, which worries whether a culture will go on valuing the one that cannot be edited, and observes that this willingness is the harder of the two to rebuild once it has been lost.

 

• The even-handedness is equally plain. The author states that neither route is simply superior, credits recording with having democratised access, and notes that repeated listening is how most people actually come to know a piece. Concern for one side is expressed without denying the merits of the other.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 reverses the author's position entirely.

 

• Option 2 overstates it — nothing in the passage rejects recordings, and their benefits are set out at some length.

 

• Option 4 ignores the evaluative language of the closing paragraph, which shows that the author is not merely reporting.

 

NOTE

 

• Tone questions usually turn on degree. Once you have decided that the author favours one side, the real choice is between mildly and strongly, and the deciding evidence is whether the other side is granted any merit. Here it plainly is.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

Music reaches its listeners today by two quite different routes, and each shapes what the music is allowed to be. A recording is made in fragments, assembled, corrected and then fixed. Its virtue is exactness: a wrong note can be removed, a tempo steadied, a balance adjusted until every instrument sits precisely where the producer intends. What the listener finally hears is a version that has never existed in a single unbroken moment, and one that will sound the same on every hearing for as long as the file survives.

 

A live performance offers the opposite bargain. Nothing can be corrected, and nothing will recur. The tempo shifts with the temper of the hall, a phrase is stretched because the audience has gone unusually quiet, and a small error passes unrepaired into the shape of the evening. Musicians describe the difference as that between a photograph and a conversation. The recording preserves; the concert responds.

 

Neither route is simply superior, though partisans of each speak as though it were. Defenders of recording point out that it democratised access: a listener in a small town can now hear performances once confined to a few metropolitan halls, and can hear them repeatedly, which is how most people actually come to know a piece. Defenders of live music reply that endless correction has bred a public intolerant of imperfection, and that a generation raised on flawless files now hears the small human unevenness of a concert as a fault rather than as the point.

 

The real question is not which format ought to survive. It is whether a culture that can afford both will go on valuing the one that cannot be edited. Access is easily measured and easily funded; the willingness to sit in a hall and accept whatever happens is neither, and it is the harder of the two to rebuild once it has been lost.

 

What is the central concern raised in the passage?
option_1: Which of the two formats will earn more revenue in future
option_2: Whether a culture will continue to value the format that cannot be edited
option_3: How recordings can be made to sound more like live performances
option_4: Why concert halls have become too expensive to maintain
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Whether a culture will continue to value the format that cannot be edited.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The final paragraph states the question in as many words: the real question is not which format ought to survive, but whether a culture that can afford both will go on valuing the one that cannot be edited.

 

• The author sharpens the point by contrasting what is easy to measure with what is not: access is easily measured and easily funded, whereas the willingness to accept whatever happens in a hall is neither. The concern is therefore about values, not about formats.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 reduces the argument to revenue, a subject the passage does not raise.

 

• Option 3 proposes a technical fix, whereas the author's point is that the two formats offer different bargains and cannot be merged.

 

• Option 4 takes up the cost of concert halls, which is nowhere discussed.

 

NOTE

 

• A sentence of the form "The real question is not X. It is Y." is the clearest possible signal of a central-idea question, and the answer is always Y. SSC reliably builds a distractor out of X.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The both boys were awarded certificates at the annual function.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Both the boys.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Both" always comes before the definite article, never after it. The correct order is both + the + plural noun.

◦ Corrected sentence: Both the boys were awarded certificates at the annual function.
◦ Example: Both the candidates cleared the interview.

 

• Two other forms are equally correct: "both boys" (article dropped) and "both of the boys" (with of before the article). What is never possible is the both.

 

• Note also that with a pronoun, of is compulsory: both of us, both of them — not both us.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 repeats the original error of placing the before both.

 

• Option 3: "both of boys" omits the article, which is required after of.

 

• Option 4: "The both of boy" compounds the wrong order with a singular noun.

 

NOTE

 

• The same rule of position governs all and half: all the students, half the class — never the all students or the half class. These determiners stand outside the article, not inside it.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

There were less students in the examination hall than the office had expected.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. fewer students.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The distinction is one of countability:

◦ "Fewer" is used with countable nouns — fewer students, fewer files, fewer mistakes.
◦ "Less" is used with uncountable nouns — less water, less time, less information.

 

• "Students" is a countable plural noun, so "fewer" is required.

◦ Corrected sentence: There were fewer students in the examination hall than the office had expected.
◦ Compare: There was less noise in the hall than expected.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 repeats the original error.

 

• Option 2: "lesser" means smaller in importance or degree (a lesser offence) and is not a quantity word at all.

 

• Option 4: "few students" would change the meaning to hardly any, and it cannot be followed by than.

 

NOTE

 

• Related countable/uncountable pairs tested by SSC: many/much, number/amount, fewer/less.
◦ A large number of applicants but a large amount of money.
◦ An exception worth knowing: less is normal before measurements treated as a single quantity — less than five kilometres, less than ten years.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

The commentator said, "What a splendid catch that was!"
option_1: The commentator exclaimed with admiration that that had been a splendid catch.
option_2: The commentator said that what a splendid catch that was.
option_3: The commentator exclaimed that it is a splendid catch.
option_4: The commentator told that that was a splendid catch.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The commentator exclaimed with admiration that that had been a splendid catch.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reported sentence is exclamatory. Its rules of conversion are:

◦ The reporting verb said changes to exclaimed with joy / admiration / sorrow / regret, according to the feeling expressed.
◦ The conjunction "that" is added.
◦ The exclamatory word "What a" is dropped and the sentence is rewritten as an assertive one.
◦ The exclamation mark disappears, and the tense is backshifted: was → had been.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 keeps the exclamatory phrase "what a splendid catch" inside a that-clause, so the sentence has not been converted at all.

 

• Option 3 fails to backshift the tense and drops the word conveying the feeling.

 

• Option 4 uses "told" without an object; told must be followed by the listener (told us that …).

 

NOTE

 

• Reporting verbs for exclamatory sentences: exclaimed with joy (Hurrah!), exclaimed with sorrow (Alas!), exclaimed with wonder (What a …!), exclaimed with regret, and applauded or cursed where appropriate. The choice of verb must match the emotion in the original.

question:
A sentence is provided in indirect speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding direct speech.

 

The storekeeper enquired where I had kept the duplicate receipt.
option_1: "Where had you kept the duplicate receipt?" the storekeeper enquired.
option_2: "Where you have kept the duplicate receipt?" the storekeeper enquired.
option_3: "Where I have kept the duplicate receipt?" the storekeeper enquired.
option_4: "Where have you kept the duplicate receipt?" the storekeeper enquired.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. "Where have you kept the duplicate receipt?" the storekeeper enquired.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is a Wh- question reported with enquired. Converting it back to direct speech reverses the usual rules:

◦ Restore the question order — the auxiliary comes before the subject.
◦ Undo the backshift: had kept → have kept.
◦ Change the pronoun back: I → you, the person addressed.
◦ End with a question mark, and enclose the words in inverted commas.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 restores the question order but leaves the tense backshifted as had kept.

 

• Option 2 keeps statement order (where you have kept), which is not possible in a direct question.

 

• Option 3 keeps the pronoun "I", so the storekeeper appears to be asking himself.

 

NOTE

 

• The two conversions are mirror images of each other:
◦ Direct → Indirect: drop the question order, drop the question mark, backshift the tense.
◦ Indirect → Direct: restore the question order, restore the question mark, undo the backshift.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. For eleven years Shanta noted in a school exercise book every bird she saw from her verandah.

 

A. A visiting researcher, shown the books by the headmaster, recognised at once what they were.

 

B. The entries were dated, timed and, wherever she was unsure of the species, marked with a question mark.

 

C. Her record now sits in a national database, credited by name.

 

D. They amounted to the longest continuous bird count anywhere in the district.

 

S2. Two of the species she listed had not been reported in the region for forty years.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. B-A-D-C.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – B – A – D – C – S2. The paragraph follows a practice → discovery → significance → outcome order.

 

• S1 describes the practice — eleven years of daily entries.

◦ B elaborates that practice, telling us how the entries were made. It belongs immediately after S1 because it introduces no new event.
◦ A brings the discovery — the researcher who recognised what the books were.
◦ D states their significance, and the pronoun "They" refers to the books just examined, so D must follow A.
◦ C gives the outcome — the record now in a national database — and leads into S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (A-B-D-C) introduces the researcher before the reader knows what the books contain.

 

• Option 3 (B-D-A-C) states the significance before anyone has examined the record, so "They" in D has no clear reference.

 

• Option 4 (A-D-B-C) places the description of the entries after their significance has already been declared.

 

NOTE

 

• A reliable principle in narrative rearrangement: description settles before action begins. Sentences that merely elaborate the opening situation come first; sentences that move the story forward follow.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. A vacuum flask keeps a liquid hot by attacking each of the three ways in which heat escapes.

 

A. With no air left in that gap, there is almost nothing for heat to travel through or travel with.

 

B. Conduction and convection are dealt with first, by the near-vacuum sealed between the two glass walls.

 

C. What little heat still escapes leaves through the narrow stopper at the top.

 

D. Radiation is then reduced by the mirrored silver coating on both the facing surfaces.

 

S2. That is why a flask left overnight is warm rather than hot by morning.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. B-A-D-C.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – B – A – D – C – S2. The paragraph explains a mechanism, and S1 announces that three routes of heat loss will be taken in turn.

 

• B is the first of the three, and the word "first" marks it as such: the vacuum deals with conduction and convection.

◦ A must follow B, since "that gap" refers to the space between the two glass walls named there.
◦ D is the second route, and the word "then" confirms that it comes after the first has been dealt with.
◦ C is the third and last — the small remainder escaping through the stopper — and it leads directly into the qualification in S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (A-B-D-C) opens with "that gap" before any gap has been mentioned.

 

• Option 2 (B-D-A-C) separates B from A, so that gap again loses its reference.

 

• Option 4 (D-B-A-C) begins with "then", which cannot open a sequence.

 

NOTE

 

• Three markers settle this question without any knowledge of physics: the ordinal "first" in B, the demonstrative "that gap" in A, and the sequencing word "then" in D. Ordinals and demonstratives are the most dependable clues in any process paragraph.
